title: Ahiram sarcophagus: Byblos inscription (KAI 1), maker's dedication
ask_addressed: Quote the primary inscriptions and texts for writing and science transmission (Ahiram sarcophagus)
quote: This coffin [Pil]sibaʿal (or: [I]ttobaʿal) has made, the son of Aḥirom (Aḥiram), King of Byblos,
summary: The 38-word Phoenician text on the rim and lid names the maker (a son of Ahiram, king of Byblos) and the dead king; the page calls it the oldest Phoenician-alphabet witness of considerable length. It is a text of the Phoenician script itself, not a record of any transfer.
limits: Wikipedia reproduces Krahmalkov's English; the reading of the son's name is uncertain ([Pil]sibaal or [I]ttobaal). Date disputed: 'around 1000 BCE' (Cook 1994, as cited on the page) versus c. 850 BCE or the 9th-8th century (Porada 1973, Wallenfels 1983, per the page). I opened only the Wikipedia compilation, not Lehmann 2005 or Cook 1994.

text.language: Old Phoenician (Byblian dialect), quoted in English (Krahmalkov translation as given on Wikipedia)
text.edition: Wikipedia 'Ahiram sarcophagus', Phoenician transliteration and Krahmalkov 2000 translation

text.witness: The sarcophagus itself, found 1923 by P. Montet in tomb V, royal necropolis of Byblos; now National Museum of Beirut (per the page).

title: Dipylon inscription (Dipylon oinochoe, Athens)
ask_addressed: Quote the primary inscriptions and texts for writing and science transmission (Dipylon oinochoe)
quote: Whoever of all these dancers now plays most delicately,
summary: A hexameter line scratched on an Attic Late Geometric jug, offered as the oldest or one of the oldest samples of Greek alphabetic writing, with letter shapes still close to Phoenician. The passage is about dancing, not about the alphabet.
limits: Wikipedia's literal translation; the text after the first 35 letters is fragmentary and its reading is uncertain. The page does not itself give the dating argument (the jug is placed in the Late Geometric style). Further reading it cites (Powell 1988; Binek 2017, a text-or-decoration debate) was not opened.

text.language: Ancient Greek (early Attic alphabet), quoted in English literal translation

composition.basis: Wikipedia: jug attributed to the Late Geometric Period 750-700 BC, inscription 'circa 740 BC'. Style-based; no scholarly dating article opened.

text.witness: The vessel itself, found 1871 near the Dipylon Gate, Kerameikos; National Archaeological Museum, Athens (NAMA 192).

title: Nestor's Cup (Pithekoussai): three-line inscription
authors: Anonymous (Wikipedia contributors); translation attributed on page to Jeffery 1963 and Faraone 1996

quote: I am the cup of Nestor good for drinking. Whoever drinks from this cup, desire for beautifully crowned Aphrodite will seize him instantly.
summary: A scratched verse on a Rhodian or Ionian cup, found in a late-8th-century cremation grave on Ischia, in the Euboean alphabet; the oldest or among the oldest Greek verse inscriptions and a witness for Greek writing in the West.
limits: The first line has a lacuna and at least fifteen proposed restorations (page); the English given is one reading. The page dates the cup 735-720 BC from the pot and grave, not from the inscription by independent means. Cited Gaunt 2017, Arrington 2021 not opened.

title: Etruscan alphabet (Marsiliana tablet and Euboean origin)
ask_addressed: Quote the primary inscriptions and texts for writing and science transmission
quote: It dates from about 700 BC, and lists 26 letters corresponding to contemporary forms of the Greek alphabet
summary: States that the earliest Etruscan abecedarium (Marsiliana tablet, ivory, 26 letters incl. digamma, san, qoppa, no omega) dates from about 700 BC and that the Etruscan alphabet is an adaptation of the Euboean alphabet of the Greek colonies at Pithekoussai and Cumae.
limits: Encyclopedia summary; the route (Pithekoussai/Cumae) is stated, not shown by a dated chain of finds in the quoted passage. Gives about 700 BC where Mnamon gives the 8th century.

title: Herodotus, Histories 5.58 (Phoenician letters brought to Greece with Cadmus)
venue: Perseus Digital Library (Harvard University Press, Loeb-era translation)
ask_addressed: Quote the primary inscriptions and texts for writing and science transmission (Greek alphabet from Phoenicia)
quote: brought with them to Hellas, among many other kinds of learning, the alphabet, which had been unknown before this, I think, to the Greeks.
summary: Herodotus says the Phoenicians who came with Cadmus brought the alphabet to Hellas, that the Ionians learned it from them and altered the letter forms, and that the letters were called 'Phoenician'. The narrative is a Greek tradition written some three centuries after the early inscriptions, so it states the route but does not prove it.
limits: Godley's English only; the Greek was not quoted. Herodotus says 'I think', and the Cadmus link is mythic. The date range is bounded only by the author's lifespan as given on Wikipedia (c. 484 - c. 425 BC); I opened no scholarly dating of the Histories.

ask_addressed: Quote the primary inscriptions and texts for writing and science transmission

title: Al-Fihrist, 'Remarks about the Greek Script' (Cadmus and the Greek letters)
ask_addressed: Quote the primary inscriptions and texts for writing and science transmission (Fihrist; alphabet tradition)
quote: bringing sixteen letters with which the Greeks wrote.
summary: Ibn al-Nadim reports 'in some of the old histories' that the Greeks learned to write from two men who came from Egypt with sixteen letters, later extended to twenty-four. A tenth-century Arabic echo of the Cadmus tradition; it does not mention the Phoenicians in the passage read.
limits: A secondhand tradition reported in 987 CE, not evidence of the 8th-century transfer; the Egypt source differs from Herodotus (Phoenicia). OCR of Dodge's English is rough ('Aghanun' printed with stray marks); quote taken from the clean words only.

title: Al-Fihrist, ch. 7: the Aristotle dream and the books from Byzantium
ask_addressed: Quote the primary inscriptions and texts for writing and science transmission (Fihrist on the translation movement)
quote: This dream was one of the most definite reasons for the output of books.
summary: Ibn al-Nadim narrates al-Ma'mun's dream of Aristotle and calls it 'one of the most definite reasons' for the plentiful output of books; he then says al-Ma'mun asked the Byzantine emperor for old scientific manuscripts and sent men to fetch and translate them.
limits: The dream is a story, and Gutas (see his own candidate) reads it as ideology, not the cause of the translation movement. This is the Fihrist's account, written about 987, over a century and a half after the events.

title: Al-Fihrist, 'Account of the Book Almagest' (Arabic translators)
ask_addressed: Quote the primary inscriptions and texts for writing and science transmission (Fihrist; Almagest)
quote: The first person to become interested in translating it and issuing it in Arabic was
summary: Says the Almagest has thirteen sections and that Yahya ibn Khalid ibn Barmak was first to want it translated into Arabic; names later translators (al-Hajjaj ibn Matar, al-Nayrizi, Ishaq ibn Hunayn, Thabit ibn Qurra correcting). It dates the Arabic Almagest to the Abbasid translation movement.
limits: The name 'Barak' is OCR for Barmak; no dates for the translations in the passage. The Fihrist is a late list, and its Hipparchus note ('said to have been his teacher') is a tradition.

venue: Duckworth (scan of the Toomer translation, classicalliberalarts.com)

summary: Ptolemy uses dated eclipse observations from Babylon, including one in the fifth year of Nabopolassar (-620 Apr. 21/22) timed 'in Babylon', to fix the moon's apparent diameter. Shows Babylonian dated records inside the Almagest.

title: Toomer's footnote to Almagest IV.2: Ptolemy's account 'not historically accurate'
venue: Duckworth (scan of the Toomer translation, classicalliberalarts.com)
ask_addressed: Quote the primary inscriptions and texts for writing and science transmission (Almagest IV.2 caution)

title: The Strange Case of Claudius Ptolemy
ask_addressed: Quote the primary inscriptions and texts for writing and science transmission (sceptical pass on the Almagest's Babylonian eclipses)
quote: most of those early Babylonian "observations" were in fact fabricated by Ptolemy
summary: Newton argues that most of the early Babylonian 'observations' reported in the Almagest were fabricated by Ptolemy, and lists the -620 and -522 eclipses (Almagest V.14) as fabricated.
limits: A strongly sceptical view; Toomer's edition and Jones (above) treat the Babylonian records as usable evidence; Newton came to the question from navigation work at the Applied Physics Laboratory (his own account on the page) and publishes in the laboratory's technical digest; his recomputation was not reproduced here. The year is not printed on the page text (Vol. 16, No. 2). The PDF is a 9 MB scan; check_quote's layout mode merges the two columns, so the quote was confirmed in plain pdftotext of the same URL.

strand.what: dated eclipse observations (alleged to be fabricated)

title: The Algebra of Mohammed ben Musa, Arabic preface (Rosen translation)
authors: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi; ed. and trans. F. Rosen
venue: Oriental Translation Fund, London (scan on archive.org)
ask_addressed: Give composition or inscription date with basis, the object or manuscript witness, and the edition read.
quote: has encouraged me to compose a short work on Calculating by (the rules of) Completion and Reduction, confining it to what is easiest
summary: In his preface al-Khwarizmi says the caliph al-Ma'mun's love of science encouraged him to write a short work on calculating by Completion and Reduction, confined to what is easiest and most useful for inheritance, trade and surveying. It is the opening of the earliest surviving Arabic algebra.
limits: Rosen's 1831 English; the text was copied in 1342 CE, five centuries after composition. The preface does not mention Indian or Greek sources.

title: The Algebra of Mohammed ben Musa, Rosen's introduction (Hindu or Diophantine source?)
venue: Oriental Translation Fund, London (scan on archive.org)

summary: Rosen argues that al-Khwarizmi's rules resemble Diophantus and the Hindu mathematicians, that the Arabs had no Diophantus until after the 4th century of the Hijra, and so it is far more probable they got algebra from the Hindus; he also says al-Khwarizmi's method of exposition is independent of the Hindus.
